title: Cheapest Trip Within a Time Limit
statement:
There are n towns numbered 0 to n − 1, where n = fees.length. Each entry roads[i] = [u, v, t] is a two-way road between towns u and v that takes t minutes to drive. Two towns may be joined by several roads.

Every time you are in a town, including the town you start in and the town you finish in, you pay that town's fee fees[town]. Visiting a town twice means paying twice.

You start in town 0 and must reach town n − 1 in at most maxTime minutes in total. Return the smallest total fee of such a trip, or -1 if no trip is fast enough.

examples.why: Going 0 → 2 → 3 takes 9 minutes and costs 3 + 1 + 2 = 6. It is the slower route, but it fits.
Now the cheap route is too slow. Only 0 → 1 → 3 (4 minutes) fits, costing 3 + 10 + 2. A plain cheapest-path search that ignores time would answer 6.

constraints: All towns are connected; no road joins a town to itself
hints: The cheapest route and the fastest route can be different routes. What extra piece of information must a search state carry so that it can respect the time limit?
Make the state (town, minutes used). The time budget is at most 1000, so you can fill a table: best[t][town] = cheapest fee to stand in town after exactly t minutes.
Or run Dijkstra by fee, with the time spent carried along. When a town is popped again, the new path costs at least as much as the earlier one, so it is only worth expanding if it arrived faster.

explain.intuition:
A cheapest-path search on fees alone can pick a route that is too slow, and a fastest-path search can pick one that is too expensive. The fix is to put the time into the state. Since maxTime is at most 1000, a table dp[t][v], the cheapest fee to be in town v after exactly t minutes, is small enough. Each road u–v taking w minutes moves you from dp[t − w][u] to dp[t][v], adding fees[v].

Dijkstra over fees is usually faster in practice. Pop states in order of fee; each carries the time already spent. The first pop of the destination is the answer. When a town comes off the heap a second time, its fee is no lower than before, so it can only help if it got there sooner. Keeping the fastest arrival time per popped town prunes everything else.
steps: Build an adjacency list with both directions of every road.
Push (fee = fees[0], time = 0, town = 0) on a min-heap ordered by fee.
Pop the cheapest state. If the town is n − 1, return its fee. If an earlier pop of this town arrived at the same time or sooner, skip it; otherwise record this time for the town.
For every road from the town whose time keeps the total within maxTime, push the neighbour with the fee and time added.
pitfalls: Marking a town as finished after its first pop, as in plain Dijkstra. A pricier but faster arrival can still be the only way to finish in time.
Forgetting the start town's fee. You pay for town 0 too.
Adding only one direction of each road, or keeping only one road between two towns when several exist with different times.

complexity.time: O(maxTime · (n + E)) for the table; Dijkstra is usually much less

solutions.title: Table over minutes and towns
solutions.idea: dp[t][v] = cheapest fee to be in town v after exactly t minutes. Relax every road for every t; the answer is the minimum of dp[t][n−1].

solutions.title: Dijkstra by fee, pruned by arrival time
solutions.idea: Pop states cheapest first. A town popped again is only worth expanding if it arrived faster than every earlier pop of it.
solutions.time: O(maxTime · E · log) worst case, far less in practice

followups: Also return the route itself. What do you store alongside each state?
Fees are only paid the first time you enter a town. Why does that make the problem much harder?
lcTitle: Minimum Cost to Reach Destination in Time
